title: Outliers: detecting them, understanding them and deciding

videos.script: Every data set has a few values that sit apart from the rest. A delivery that took three times as long as the others. A basket worth twenty ordinary ones. {{apart}} The tempting move is to delete them and get on with it. The data looks tidier, the mean looks more sensible, and nobody asks questions. {{tempting}} That move throws away information, and sometimes the most important information in the table. {{information}} An outlier can be three different things. A mistake: a decimal point in the wrong place. A visitor from another population: a restaurant ordering eighty kilos of tomatoes from a shop that serves households. Or a genuine extreme: a family doing its biggest shop of the year. {{three}} Each one calls for a different response. The mistake gets corrected. The visitor gets analysed separately. The genuine extreme stays, because it is part of what you are trying to describe. {{responses}} This lesson gives you three ways to find candidates, explains why the most popular one can fail exactly when you need it, and ends with a rule that never changes. Whatever you decide, you write it down. {{write}}
